body:
# Independent audit: generic-budget normal full-cover hinge stress

Audited source: `candidate 2d0fea5cdbf7c841`, including
the exact sensitivity addition (6a)--(6b). Result: **PASS**, with the scope
exactly as stated in that note. This is a normality theorem for a fixed
finite family of positive full-dimensional polytope fibers and a fixed
number of caps. It is not an OC inequality.

## 1. Attainment and the value function

The imported trace-saturation argument is applicable. Positivity of each
fiber volume bounds each affine fiber threshold below along a bounded
hinge sequence. After taking a subsequence, each threshold has a finite
limit or tends to positive infinity. The finite-coordinate restriction of
the affine trace space is a finite-dimensional closed subspace. Thus the
finite limits have an exact affine extension. Correcting the approximating
traces by a bounded right inverse leaves a kernel sequence, zero on the
finite coordinates and tending to positive infinity on all remaining
coordinates. One sufficiently late member of this sequence, suitably
scaled, makes all those remaining caps empty while preserving the exact
finite limits. This gives finite parameters at the limit.

Cap masses and hinges converge on every finite trace because the continuous
normal stays nonzero. Its boundary has zero fiber volume, including when
it supports a facet. For each fixed point of each fiber, some cap covers
that point along an infinite subsequence; that cap cannot have an infinite
threshold and its limiting closed cap still contains the point. Hence
coverage passes. No unjustified uniform convergence of covering indices
is needed.

The finite clipped-polytope decomposition gives semialgebraic cap volumes,
first moments, and hinges. Full-dimensional simplex determinants have
rational expressions in the cap coefficients on each of finitely many
combinatorial pieces; lower-dimensional pieces contribute zero volume.
The min-max coverage value is semialgebraic by its finite LP, or by real
quantifier elimination. Quantifying attained optimality consequently gives
the graph of the actual value function, not merely a graph of candidate
critical values. One-variable semialgebraic regularity gives a finite
partition into open intervals on which that function is C1. This does not
assert continuity at the finitely many exceptional budgets or at feasible
endpoints.

## 2. Local Lipschitz bounds and the two penalties

The local cap-mass bound is valid even at supporting facets: membership can
change only in a slab of thickness proportional to the parameter change,
whose volume is controlled by a bounded orthogonal projection area. In
dimension one this projection measure is counting measure on a point.
The hinge is C1 because each actual cap boundary has zero fiber volume.
The coverage value is locally Lipschitz by taking the min and max after a
uniform bound on the change of the finitely many affine margins.

The coverage repair has the exact sign and size claimed:

`b_i -> b_i-G` implies `F_z -> F_z+G` and distance `sqrt(N)G`.

It keeps every unit continuous normal fixed, so it stays on the parameter
manifold. At a regular budget, the value-function Lipschitz bound proves
the first exact penalty only for nearby covers, which is precisely the
input needed for the repair. The repair then proves a local unconstrained
minimum on the sphere manifold for the second penalty. Neither step needs
strict feasibility of the original cap budgets or a constraint
qualification. The coefficient of the differentiable hinge objective is
one before any generalized-gradient argument is applied.

The stronger penalty `Psi-v(s)` is valid when the cap budget is active:
`s` remains in the open regular interval near the minimizer, and every
nearby cover has `Psi>=v(s)`. The chain and maximum rules give nonnegative
cap multipliers whose sum satisfies

`M sum_i r_i=-v'(tau)`.

If the chosen minimizer has slack budget, it remains feasible throughout
an interval immediately below `tau`. Monotonicity and its optimality force
the value to be constant there; differentiability gives `v'(tau)=0`.
The direct hinge-and-coverage penalty then supplies `r_i=0`. Thus the
exact sensitivity formula covers both cases.

## 3. Generalized gradients and true contacts

The sphere constraints cause no missing gradient components. Apply
Clarke Fermat in smooth charts, then the chain, sum, and maximum
inclusions for ambient locally Lipschitz functions. The resulting ambient
sum is normal to the product of spheres, giving one unrestricted scalar
multiple of each `u_i`. For `d=1`, the sphere is locally a point, so its
normal space is the whole one-dimensional continuous-normal coordinate,
which is consistent with the same conclusion.

The cap-gradient representation is valid with one section measure per
chosen cap gradient. Regular nearby sections project onto the limiting
plane with Jacobians tending to one; their weak limits are dominated by
the limiting section's Hausdorff measure. Proper sections have density
one almost everywhere. Supporting-facet limits and their convex
combinations may have nonconstant densities in `[0,1]`. All zeroth and
first moments must be taken from that same density, as the source does.
The support-plane moment identity is therefore exact.

For coverage, the parameterized finite LP has optimal primal vertices
and optimal dual solutions. On its generic full-dimensional cells one
can fix optimal bases, differentiate their rational solutions, and cancel
the primal variation by dual stationarity. This yields
`lambda_i(z,x,-1)`. The nongeneric cells can be excluded in computing the
Clarke gradient. Primal points remain in compact `K_z` and the cap dual
weights remain in the compact simplex. Any limiting pair is an actual
saddle pair because the margins and the optimal value are continuous.
The convex hull of this compact feature image is compact, so finite
Caratheodory representations suffice.

At `F_z=0`, a primal optimizer has every margin nonpositive, and a dual
optimizer has weighted average zero. Hence every positive dual weight
is carried by an actual zero margin. The normal-cone sign is also
correct: minimizing the weighted affine margin gives
`-sum_i lambda_i u_i in N_Kz(x)` for the usual outward normal cone.

The separate moments `p_zi=int lambda_i` and
`q_zi=int lambda_i x` are essential. The proof does not replace their
finite saddle-pair measure by a product of one point and one set of
weights. Thus all retained contacts belong to the actual fibers, even
when different caps use different points of the same fiber.

## 4. Signs, normalization, and Euler cancellation

Writing stationarity for the objective, cap budgets, and `-F_z` gives
exactly (13)--(15). In particular the offset coordinate is

`-c_i-r_i S_i+sum_z eta_z p_zi=0`,

which confirms the total-mass sign. Taking the scalar combination with
`(a_i,u_i,-b_i)` yields the cap hinge, zero section contribution, zero
contact contribution, and the sphere multiplier. Therefore

`sigma_i=-Psi_i`,
`X_i+r_i X_i^s=sum_z eta_z q_zi+Psi_i u_i`.

The objective multiplier is one, and the moment equations retain all
supporting-fiber normal forces. They imply equality of total and integer
first moments of the two indicated measures, plus the stated continuous
moment difference. They do not imply convex order or a sign for integer
transport flux.

The finite exceptional set is independent of the chosen minimizer at a
regular budget. No conclusion is made at the minimum feasible budget,
for nonpolyhedral fibers, under changes in the cap count, or about a
uniform bound for `-v'(tau)`. These exclusions are necessary and are
preserved in the audited statement.
note: Mathematical discussion retained to expose corrections and limitations. This is not a verification run, accepted premise, or approval of the revised submission. Association follows explicit source-document references, not an inferred dependency.
